title: Rounding the weights to a grid: step size, error bounds, and how the error travels through a network and a rollout
summary: Quantization replaces each weight by the nearest point of a grid with $2^b$ levels. The error of one weight is at most half a grid step, the error of a layer output grows like the square root of the number of inputs in practice and at worst linearly, and in a rollout it is shaped by the stability of the dynamics. Every extra bit halves the error, and a fair comparison fixes the bit budget and checks the whole rolled-out trajectory, not one step.

source.note: Standard numerical analysis and fixed-point arithmetic. The figure is the design system's synthetic F7.6 ablation render, used as a picture of a comparison against a baseline with intervals, not as a result. All numbers were computed for this page with NumPy and SciPy on random weights and a random stable linear system.

read_the_figure.question: Which change makes the metric worse than the full model by more than the noise, and which is within the noise?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the metric, higher is better, mean with a 95 percent interval over 10 seeds. y: the full model and variants with one component removed.
look_at: The dashed baseline and the shaded band around it: variants whose interval touches the band are not different from the full model.
The longest drop (component 4) against the near-baseline variants (components 3 and 5).
The width of each interval: wide ones need more seeds before a ranking is meaningful.
Whether every variant has the same budget: one component fewer saves bits or time, which matters for a fair comparison.
read_the_figure.proves: That removing some components changes the metric by more than the seed noise and removing others does not. It does not prove that the remaining components are necessary together or that the result holds with another dataset.
if_wrong: Intervals omitted: a difference of 0.01 cannot be told from noise.
Different budgets between the arms: the baseline is not a fair comparison.
Quantised and unquantised arms evaluated on a one-step error while the claim is about rollouts.
must_check: Same data and budget in every arm.
The metric that the claim is about (the rollout, not a step).

terms.meaning: Replacing each value by the nearest point of a finite grid, here a uniform grid of $2^b$ levels over a range.
The number of bits $b$ per weight; the grid has $2^b$ levels.
The spacing of the grid over the range $[-1,1]$.
The difference between a value and its nearest grid point; at most half the step.
How much the output changes when the weights change by a small amount; it decides how rounding errors amplify.
The distance between the original and the quantised model after integrating both over time.
The total number of bits spent on the model: parameters times bits. Comparisons are fair at equal budget.
The error level at which a rollout of a contracting system stops growing, set by the error per step divided by the decay rate.

remember: On a uniform grid with $2^b$ levels over $[-1,1]$ the step is $\Delta=2/2^b$ and the largest rounding error of a weight is $\Delta/2$. For 8 bits: step 0.0078, error at most 0.0039.
Rounding errors of independent weights are about uniform on $[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$ with standard deviation $\Delta/\sqrt{12}$.
For a layer $y=Wx$ with $n$ inputs of size at most 1, the worst-case output error is $n\Delta/2$; the typical error is about $\sqrt{n}\,\Delta\,\mathrm{rms}(x)/\sqrt{12}$.
One more bit halves $\Delta$, so it halves the error to first order.

In a rollout of a stable linear system $\dot y=Ay$, quantizing $A$ changes its eigenvalues by about $\|\delta A\|$ times the eigenvector condition number, and the error in the trajectory is bounded by that shift times time, up to the decay.
A fair comparison fixes the total bits and the metric, and evaluates the full trajectory.

understand.title: Easy: measuring with a ruler that has coarse marks
understand.text: If a ruler is marked only to the nearest centimetre, every length you write down is off by at most half a centimetre. Add up a hundred such lengths and the errors partly cancel, so the total is typically off by about ten times that, not a hundred times. A finer ruler (one more bit) halves every mark's error.

understand.title: Medium: bound against typical
understand.text: Writing each weight as the true value plus an error in $[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$, a dot product of $n$ terms picks up an error of at most $n\Delta/2$ if all errors line up with the signs of the inputs. They almost never do: signs are random, so the typical error grows like $\sqrt n$. Both numbers are useful: the bound is a guarantee and the typical value is what you will see.

understand.title: Hard: through time the dynamics decide
understand.text: In a rollout the error made at each step is carried forward by the dynamics. If the system contracts, errors die away and the error saturates at the per-step error over the decay rate; if it is neutral they add up linearly; if it is unstable they grow exponentially. Quantizing the right-hand side also moves the eigenvalues, so a marginally stable model can become unstable or the other way round. A step-by-step error can look harmless and still give a wrong trajectory.

understand.title: Hardest: a fair comparison
understand.text: A quantised model with fewer bits is smaller, so the question is what you get for the same size. Compare at equal total bits: more parameters at fewer bits against fewer parameters at more. Use the same data, the same metric (the rolled-out error against the reference), several seeds with intervals and, where relevant, the same solver and step. Without that, differences between formats are tangled with differences in budget.

steps.title: A uniform grid over [-1, 1]
steps.note: At 4 bits $\Delta=0.125$, at 8 bits $0.0078$, at 12 bits $0.00049$. The measured largest error over 1024 random weights equalled $\Delta/2$ to three digits at every width (computed), as it should.

steps.title: The error of one layer: bound and typical value
steps.note: For $n=32$ inputs at 8 bits the bound is 0.125, the largest output error observed was 0.0131 and the rms error 0.0067 against a prediction of 0.0075 (computed, random $W\in[-1,1]^{32\times32}$ and $x\in[-1,1]^{32}$). The bound is a worst case ten times larger than what happens.

steps.title: Each bit halves the error
steps.note: The rms output error was 0.121, 0.0249, 0.00669, 0.00208 and 0.00048 for 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 bits (computed): a factor 4 per 2 bits to within the scatter of one random draw.

steps.title: A rollout of a linear model
steps.note: A random stable $4\times4$ matrix with entries in $[-1,1]$ and largest real eigenvalue $-0.772$ was rounded to each width and both models integrated to $T=10$ by matrix exponential from $y_0=(1,1,1,1)$.

steps.title: The trajectory error
steps.note: The maximum error over the run was 0.105, 0.0556, 0.0270, 0.0134 and 0.0016 for 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 bits (computed): a factor 1.9, 2.1, 2.0 between consecutive widths and 8.4 between 6 and 8 bits. The error follows the grid step, as the bound says, and stays bounded because the model contracts.

steps.title: Eigenvalues move with the rounding
steps.note: The largest real eigenvalue moved from $-0.772$ to $-0.750$ at 3 bits, $-0.818$ at 4 bits and $-0.773$ at 8 bits (computed). A system that is only weakly stable can cross zero with a coarse grid, so check the eigenvalues of the quantised model as well as its output.

steps.title: The comparison at equal bit budget
steps.note: Eight bits on one weight matrix against four bits on two matrices of the same total size are different models with the same budget. Report the rolled-out error against the reference with intervals over seeds, as in the ablation dot plot: a variant is better only if its interval clears the baseline band.

worked.title: How many bits keep a layer's output error below 0.01?
worked.problem: A layer $y=Wx$ has $n=32$ inputs with $|x_j|\le1$ and weights in $[-1,1]$. Find the grid step and the guaranteed bound for 8 and 10 bits, the typical rms error, and decide which width is needed for 0.01 as a guarantee and as a typical value.
worked.answer: Typical error: 8 bits already gives about 0.007, below 0.01 (measured rms 0.0067). Guarantee: the worst-case bound needs $\Delta\le0.000625$, hence 12 bits (calculated). The four extra bits are the price of a guarantee against the case where every rounding error lines up with the sign of its input, which did not occur in the measurement.

analyze.q: The rollout error of a quantised stable model flattens at a constant level. What sets that level and how does it change with one more bit?
analyze.hint: Per-step error over decay rate; the step halves.

analyze.q: A marginally stable oscillator is quantised and its amplitude grows slowly. Explain without any new numerics.
analyze.hint: The rounded matrix has eigenvalues moved a little to the right.

analyze.q: Why can 8-bit arithmetic on 64 inputs give a similar relative error to 8 bits on 16 inputs, although the bound is 4 times larger?
analyze.hint: The typical error grows like the square root of n and so does the signal.

evaluate.q: A report compares a 4-bit model with 4000 parameters and an 8-bit model with 1000 parameters and calls the 8-bit one more accurate. What is missing?
evaluate.hint: Equal bit budget, same metric on rollouts, intervals over seeds.

evaluate.q: Is the worst-case bound useless because it is ten times larger than what you observe?
evaluate.hint: When is a guarantee needed instead of a typical value?

create: Design a test that finds the smallest bit width at which the rolled-out trajectory error of a trained model stays inside the seed noise of the unquantised model.
Propose a way to quantise different layers with different widths under a total bit budget and say how to choose them.
Sketch the plot that shows rollout error against bit width with the worst-case bound as a second line.

checks.q: Why is the rounding error of a weight at most half the grid step?
checks.answer: Every value lies between two adjacent grid points a step $\Delta$ apart. The nearest one is at most $\Delta/2$ away, and the value halfway between is at exactly $\Delta/2$.

checks.q: What is the grid step and the largest rounding error at 6 bits over [-1,1]?
checks.answer: $\Delta=2/64=0.03125$ and the largest error is $0.0156$ (calculated; measured maximum 0.01561).

checks.q: Why is the typical error of a layer smaller than its bound?
checks.answer: The bound assumes every weight error has the sign that adds to the output. Rounding errors are close to independent and uniformly signed, so they partly cancel and their sum grows like $\sqrt n$ rather than $n$. For $n=32$ at 8 bits the bound was 0.125 and the rms error 0.0067.

checks.q: A quantised model matches the original to 1e-3 on a single step. Does that justify using it for a long rollout?
checks.answer: No. A contracting model forgets the step error, but a neutral one accumulates it linearly and an unstable one exponentially, and quantizing the right-hand side also shifts the eigenvalues. Roll out the quantised model for the full horizon from several starts and compare with the reference.

checks.q: How would you pick the bit width for a trained rate network that will be used in a simulation of length T?
checks.hint: Pick a tolerance on the trajectory and test widths.
checks.answer: Choose a tolerance on the rolled-out trajectory error (for example the seed-to-seed spread of the full-precision model), quantise at 3 to 12 bits, integrate from several held-out starts for the full length $T$, and take the smallest width whose error interval stays below the tolerance. Check the eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the quantised model along the trajectory too.
